prompt: B-Tree of minimum degree t — which two statements are correct?
options: Every node except the root holds between t−1 and 2t−1 keys.
All leaves lie at the same depth, so a B-Tree is height-balanced by construction.
A node with k keys has exactly k children.
The root must hold at least t−1 keys, like every other node.
explanation: The key-count bounds ✓ and the equal-depth property ✓ are definitional. A node with k keys has k+1 children — the extra child covers the range beyond the last key ✗ — and the root is the explicit exception, needing only 1 key ✗.

prompt: Why are B-Trees used for disk-backed storage? Which two statements are correct?
options: Many keys per node keep the tree very shallow, so few disk accesses are needed.
A fetch from memory takes much longer than a comparison, so comparing many keys already loaded in one node is cheap.
B-Trees need fewer comparisons in total than a BST holding the same keys.
B-Trees avoid pointers entirely, so no memory addresses have to be resolved.
explanation: Low height ⟹ few fetches ✓, and "fetch takes longer than compare" is exactly the architectural argument from the lecture ✓. A B-Tree may well perform *more* comparisons than a BST — it just performs far fewer expensive fetches ✗ — and it still uses child pointers ✗.

prompt: Which idea allows B-Tree insert to be a single top-to-bottom pass with no backtracking?
options: Every full node encountered is preemptively split *before* the algorithm descends into it.
Insertion always happens at the root, and a background process rebalances later.
Excess keys are kept in a separate overflow list.
Only leaves that were pre-allocated with spare capacity are used.
explanation: Checking and splitting a child before descending guarantees that the leaf finally reached is non-full, so no split is ever required on the way back up. This is the exact mirror image of delete's "ensure ≥ t keys before descending" rule.

prompt: A full node c (2t−1 keys) with parent x is split. Which two statements are correct?
options: The median key — the t-th key of c — moves up into x at its correct sorted position.
The remaining 2t−2 keys split evenly: t−1 stay in c, t−1 move into a new right sibling.
The median key is discarded, since it is now represented by the split point.
All 2t−1 keys move into the new sibling, leaving c empty.
explanation: Promoting the median ✓ and splitting the remainder evenly into t−1 / t−1 ✓ is the split operation. If c was internal, its 2t children likewise split t / t. Nothing is discarded ✗ and c is never emptied ✗.

prompt: B-Tree delete: while descending, the child c you must enter has exactly t−1 keys and an immediate sibling has ≥ t keys. What happens before descending?
options: Borrow: the separating key rotates from the parent down into c, and the sibling's adjacent extreme key moves up into the parent.
Merge c with that sibling regardless of its key count.
Nothing — t−1 keys is enough to descend into.
c is removed and its keys are redistributed across the whole level.
explanation: Borrowing (a rotation through the parent) gives c a spare key without merging, and is preferred whenever a sibling can afford it. Merging is the fallback used only when *both* siblings have exactly t−1 keys.

prompt: B-Tree delete: key k lies in the internal node x, and both the child before k and the child after k have exactly t−1 keys. What happens?
options: The left child, k and the right child are merged into one node of 2t−1 keys, then k is deleted recursively from it.
k is removed directly from x, leaving a gap.
A key is borrowed from the grandparent.
This situation cannot occur in a valid B-Tree.
explanation: Neither child can spare a key for the predecessor/successor swap (cases 2a/2b), so the only remaining option is case 2c: merge y, k and z into a single legal node of exactly 2t−1 keys and continue the deletion there.

prompt: How does a B-Tree's height change? Which two statements are correct?
options: The height grows only by splitting the root, which creates a new root holding a single key.
The height shrinks only when a merge consumes the root's last remaining key.
The height grows whenever any internal node is split.
The height shrinks whenever a leaf becomes empty.
explanation: Splitting an internal node pushes its median into an existing parent, so the depth is unchanged — only the root has no parent to absorb it, which is why the root split is the sole way to grow ✓✗. Symmetrically the root merge is the sole way to shrink ✓✗, since all leaves must stay at equal depth.

prompt: A B-Tree with minimum degree t = 2 is structurally equivalent to which classic structure?
options: A 2-3-4 tree, which is structurally equivalent to a Red-Black tree
An AVL tree
A splay tree
A binary max-heap
explanation: With t = 2 every node holds 1–3 keys and therefore has 2, 3 or 4 children — a 2-3-4 tree. The standard correspondence maps a 3-key node onto a black node with two red children, which is exactly a Red-Black tree.

prompt: Which two conditions would make a candidate tree structurally *invalid* as a B-Tree?
options: A non-root node has k keys but only k children.
Two leaves lie at different depths.
A non-root node holds exactly 2t−1 keys.
The root holds only a single key.
explanation: k keys demand exactly k+1 children ✗ and all leaves must share one depth ✗ — both are violations. A node with 2t−1 keys is merely *full*, which is legal ✓, and a single-key root is the explicit root exception ✓.
